title: Association Between Prenatal Pesticide Exposure and Executive Function in Preschool Children
content: Prenatal pesticide exposure may affect child neurodevelopment, but evidence from low- and middle-income countries remains limited. This study examined the association between maternal occupational pesticide exposure during pregnancy and executive function in children aged 4-6 years. In a cross-sectional study of 432 mother-child pairs from small-scale horticulture in three selected Tanzanian districts, mothers reported their involvement in six pesticide-related activities during pregnancy, which were summed into a composite exposure score (range 0–12). Children’s executive function was rated by parents using a 22-item adaptation of the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF), expressed as sample-standardized T-scores. Associations were estimated using multiple linear regression adjusted for child’s sex and age, mother’s age, and years in horticulture. The composite exposure score (mean ± SD; 2.6 ± 2.8), summarizing ex-posure across multiple activities, revealed exposure-dependent increases in behavioral regulation (β = 0.667, 95% CI: 0.343-0.991, p < 0.001) and global executive function scores (β = 0.494, 95% CI: 0.170-0.817, p = 0.003) after adjustment for the child’s sex, the child’s age, the mother’s age and the mother’s working years in horticulture. Higher maternal engagement in pesticide-related activities during pregnancy was found to be associated with adverse executive functioning in children. However, the findings warrant cautious interpretation and further investigation.
